fact_en:
Do antibiotics only kill bad bacteria?

Not quite — antibiotics can also kill the helpful bacteria in our gut, which is why some people get diarrhea while taking them.
fact_bis:
Dautan ra ba nga bakterya ang gipatay sa antibiotiko?

Dili diay — mapatay usab niini ang maayong bakterya sa atong tinai, mao nga usahay magtibi ang moinom niini.

findings.note: EN: antibiotics kill gut bacteria "which is why some people get diarrhea". BIS says "usahay magtibi ang moinom niini" — tibi is CONSTIPATION, the opposite symptom. The card never says kalibanga, so the fact is unrecoverable and a child learns the reverse. Corpus check confirms the sense: ffct-14019 uses 'tibi' for constipation (fiber prevents it), while diarrhea is 'kalibanga' in 32 other cards.

title_bis: Usa ka Tiil Taas, Usa Modagan
fact_en:
Why does one leg lift while the other stiffens?

Step on something sharp and your foot lifts up automatically while your other leg stiffens to hold you up — your spinal cord sends both orders at once, no thinking needed!
fact_bis:
Nganong moalsa ang usa ka tiil samtang motig-a ang isa?

Kon matumban ka og tunokon, kusganon moalsa ang tiil samtang motig-a ang pikas aron mosuporta kanimo — dungan nga nagmando ang gulugod sa duha, bisan wala nimo hunahunaa!

findings.note: title_bis 'Usa ka Tiil Taas, Usa Modagan' = 'one leg up, one RUNS', for title_en 'One Leg Lifts, One Braces'. The card's whole fact is that the other leg stiffens to hold you up (body has it right: 'motig-a ang pikas aron mosuporta'), so the title asserts the opposite action. Title-only defect, restored by the body, but it is a factual change rather than awkward wording.

fact_en: Water hyacinth, a plant different from water lilies, floats freely on the surface of rivers and lakes.
fact_bis: Ang water hyacinth, lahi sa water lily, mobangga sa ibabaw sa mga suba ug lanaw.

findings.note: EN: water hyacinth 'floats freely on the surface of rivers and lakes' — the point of the card, and what distinguishes it from the rooted water lily it is contrasted with. BIS says 'mobangga sa ibabaw sa mga suba ug lanaw' — mobangga = collides/bumps into, not floats. The floating fact is not restored anywhere else in the card. Corpus check: of 557 cards with float/floating in EN, 477 use lutaw; 'bangga' forms otherwise appear only in genuine collision cards (particles, echoes, musk ox headbutt).

fact_en: The smiling masks of the MassKara Festival copy the zygomaticus major — the muscle that pulls up the corners of our mouth.
fact_bis: Ang mga nagpahiyum nga maskara sa MassKara Festival nagsundog sa zygomaticus major — ang otot nga mopataas sa kanto sa atong baba.

findings.note: EN: zygomaticus major is 'the muscle that pulls up the corners of our mouth'. BIS renders muscle as 'otot' — in Cebuano 'otot' is fart/flatulence, not muscle. The card never uses kaunuran/unod anywhere, so a Cebuano-only reader is told the zygomaticus major is an 'otot'. Corpus check: 392 sweep cards contain 'muscle' in EN and every other one uses kaunuran/kaunoran/unod; 'otot' occurs exactly once corpus-wide, here.

fact_en: To stop termites from hollowing out wood, people place bait nearby — termites carry it back to the colony as food, wiping out the whole group.
fact_bis: Aron mapugngan ang anay sa pag-ubos sa kahoy, ibutang ang paon duol kanila — dad-on nila kini ngadto sa kolonya isip pagkaon, mao nga mapuo ang tibuok grupo.

findings.note: title_bis 'Pait sa Anay' for title_en 'Termite Bait' — 'pait' is bitter/bitterness, not bait; the body correctly uses 'paon'. English 'bait' appears to have been read as the Cebuano word 'pait'. Lower severity than ffct-05608 since the body restores 'paon' in the same sentence, but the displayed title states a different thing. Corpus check: EN 'bait' + BIS 'pait' hits exactly 2 cards, both in this batch.

fact_en: Dust mites hiding in unwashed bedding release proteins that can trigger asthma attacks and allergic reactions in sensitive children.
fact_bis: Ang mga dust mite sa dili hugot nga higdaanan nagpagawas og mga protina nga makapukaw og hika ug allergy sa sensitibong mga bata.

findings.note: EN "Dust mites hiding in unwashed bedding" -> BIS "Ang mga dust mite sa dili hugot nga higdaanan". `hugot` is tight/firm, so the Cebuano says "bedding that isn't tight" (loose bedding), not unwashed bedding (dili hinugasan/dili labhan). Nothing else in the card restores washing, so the child is left with a false attribute — that looseness of the bedding is what harbours dust mites — and loses the one actionable fact (wash the bedding). Likely a slip from `hugas`.

fact_en: Wild pigs often live together in small family groups made up of mothers and their piglets.
fact_bis: Ang mga ihalas nga baboy kasagaran nagpuyo nga magkauban sa gagmay nga pundok sa mga inahan ug nati.

findings.note: title_bis names a different topic than the card. title_en "Wild Pig Family Groups" -> title_bis "Panagway sa Ligaw nga Baboy" = 'Appearance/Looks of the wild pig'. The card is entirely about social structure ("nagpuyo nga magkauban sa gagmay nga pundok sa mga inahan ug nati"); nothing about looks. 'panagway' is unambiguously face/appearance and the corpus uses it that way 22 times ("lahi ang panagway sa managsoon", "Mausab ang panagway sa grassland"), so this is a misuse, not regional variation. Lower severity than the three above — the title is off-topic rather than false, and the body carries the fact — but the family-group idea is absent from the title a child sees. Deliberately given a slug, not a word pair: 'panagway' is correct for 'appearance' in general and a corpus-wide grep would be ~96% false hits.

fact_en:
How many bones does an adult have?

An adult human body has 206 bones.
fact_bis:
Pila ka bukog ang lawas sa usa ka hamtong?

Ang lawas sa hamtong nga tawo adunay 206 ka bukog.

findings.note: title_bis entity swap. title_en "206 Bones in Adults" -> title_bis "206 Bukog Kaban". Cebuano 'kaban' is a chest/trunk/box (or a sack of grain), never 'adult' — the title reads as '206 bones [in the] chest', a false claim about where the 206 bones are. Correct word is 'hamtong', which this card's own body uses ("Ang lawas sa hamtong nga tawo adunay 206 ka bukog") and which the corpus uses 177 times. 'kaban' has only 4 corpus hits and 3 of them are this same adult->kaban mistranslation (ffct-09441 same card, and ffct-03674 "Deep Cut Tell Adult" -> "Lalom Samat Kaban", body 'tigulang'), so the grep is almost noise-free.

fact_en:
Why can birds fly even when big?

Birds are light enough to fly because many of their bones are hollow, filled with air inside — so they aren't too heavy even when large.
fact_bis:
Ngano makalupad gihapon ang langgam bisan dako?

Gaan ang langgam aron makalupad kay hungaw ang daghan sa iyang mga bukog, may sulod nga hangin, mao nga dili kini bug-at bisan dako.

findings.note: title_bis states a false fact. title_en "Hollow Bones Light Birds" -> title_bis "Wala Bukog Langgam" = 'bird has no bones'. Birds' bones being hollow (not absent) is the whole point; the body says it correctly ("hungaw ang daghan sa iyang mga bukog, may sulod nga hangin"), but a title-only reader is told birds have no bones. Corpus evidence that 'wala' is the wrong word here: hollow is rendered 'guwang' 36x (e.g. ffct-02021 "Guwang nga Bukog sa Langgam") plus 'hawan'/'hungaw'; meanwhile 'wala bukog' is used correctly for genuinely boneless things (ffct-13375 "Organ nga Wala Bukog" = organs with no bones), which is exactly the reading it forces here. Systematic: 5 hollow-bone cards carry this same title (ffct-04281, ffct-07676, ffct-08329, ffct-10741, ffct-14140).

fact_en: Krill, small shrimp-like creatures, form the base of the ocean food chain — whales, penguins, and seals all rely on them heavily for food.
fact_bis: Ang krill, gagmay nga crustacean nga morag hipon, mao ang pundasyon sa food chain sa dagat — nagsalig kaayo ang mga balyena, penguin, ug selyo niini isip pagkaon.

findings.note: Krill food-chain card renders the animal seal as "selyo": "nagsalig kaayo ang mga balyena, penguin, ug selyo niini isip pagkaon." In Cebuano selyo is a stamp / safety seal / gasket — the same corpus uses it in exactly that sense (ffct-11108 "Tibuok nga selyo" = intact medicine safety seal; ffct-17259 rubber seals). The corpus's baby-seal card ffct-11331 keeps the English word "seal" for the animal. Nothing in this card restores it, so the child is told whales, penguins and stamps depend on krill and cannot name the third animal.

fact_en:
What is ocean acidification?

When carbon dioxide from the air dissolves into the ocean, it lowers the water's pH — making it harder for shellfish and coral to build their shells.
fact_bis:
Unsa ang ocean acidification?

Kon ang carbon dioxide gikan sa hangin matunaw sa dagat, mapaubos ang pH niini — nagpalisod sa mga shellfish ug coral sa paghimo sa ilang mga balhibo.

findings.note: Ocean acidification card: Cebuano ends "nagpalisod sa mga shellfish ug coral sa paghimo sa ilang mga balhibo" — balhibo is fur/feathers/body hair, not a shell. The corpus's own word is kabhang (e.g. ffct-05967 "Kabhang sa Hipon", ffct-06018). The Cebuano body never names a shell anywhere, so a Cebuano-only child learns that acid makes it hard for shellfish and coral to grow FUR. The only 'Shell' on the card is the untranslated English word sitting in title_bis ("Ocean Acidification Shell"), which does not repair the sentence.

fact_en:
Can a toad jump as far as a frog?

Not really — a toad has shorter legs and usually just crawls or hops a little, unlike a frog's long, far leaps.
fact_bis:
Makalukso ba ang kabakaba sama sa baki?

Dili kaayo — mas mubo ang paa sa kabakaba mao nga kasagaran mokamang lang o gamay ra molukso, lahi sa layo nga lukso sa baki.

findings.note: Toad-vs-frog card names the toad twice with words that are not toad: body "Makalukso ba ang kabakaba sama sa baki? ... mas mubo ang paa sa kabakaba", and title_bis "Baki vs Hibya sa Lukso". Corpus-wide, toad is baki, plain "toad", kamprag or kambabalod (ffct-00232 "Ang baki o toad"; the parallel toad/frog card ffct-11999 writes "toad" in Cebuano); "kabakaba" occurs nowhere else as toad and IS listed in the corpus's own terms for a BUTTERFLY card (ffct-13032, alongside alibangbang/paruparo), and "hibya" occurs nowhere else at all. A Cebuano-only child cannot tell which animal is being compared to the frog, and may read it as a butterfly with short legs. Medium confidence on the word sense — the flag rests mainly on the card naming the same animal two different non-corpus ways and never saying toad/baki for it.
